description:
The first public hall places an unexplained sabre beside coastal objects with ordinary uses: a bell, sounding weights, a shipping ledger and ceramics. The attendant distinguishes evidence from conjecture. Seeing the blade is a visit, not acquiring it.

Proposed curatorial practice: labels distinguish an object’s reported find-place from what wear and material actually show. A cracked sounding weight can be useful evidence without being valuable treasure; an incomplete shipping ledger can identify a trade route without explaining a drowned people. The missing blade leaves an empty mounting and an interrupted ordinary display, not a newly revealed altar.

links.description: Proposed late visit: bring a rubbing or careful description from a submerged threshold and compare it with an ordinary collection piece. Museum knowledge is partial; similarity supports a question, not proof of the sabre’s maker or a full account of the catastrophe.

name: Dockside Museum
